title: Hosted API: Tokenizer regression -> batching collapse postmortem
summary: On 2029-03-17 a roll-forward of a tokenizer library change caused under-counting of token lengths for a subset of input encodings. The runtime adaptive batcher packed requests into oversized batches which led to GPU OOMs on inference workers, triggering streaming connection resets and 5xx errors across multiple regions for ~2.5 hours. The outage impacted ~12% of production requests at peak, primarily small chat sessions with mixed UTF-8/legacy encodings.
impact: At peak (09:35–10:20 UTC) 12% of requests returned 5xx errors or aborted streaming sessions. P95 latency for successful requests increased from baseline 180ms to 850ms due to retry traffic and transient backpressure. Customer-facing error rate rose to ~9% for the hosted API key tier; some customers experienced streaming truncation which affected long-running assistant sessions.
timeline:
09:05 UTC — Deploy of tokenizer version 2.14.0 (roll-forward to fix edge-case trimming) to hosted-api canary cluster (auto rollout planned).
09:22 UTC — Canary telemetry shows no immediate failures; rollout continued to 50% of nodes.
09:33 UTC — First GPU OOM observed in east-us-1 worker pool; autoscaler attempted restart, which repeatedly failed on the new image.
09:35 UTC — Streaming session resets spike; alerts fired for elevated 5xx and p95 latency.
09:38 UTC — Oncall paged; investigation begins.
09:45 UTC — Correlation between OOMs and high token_count_sent metrics identified; heuristic showed many requests with token_count underestimated by ~25%.
09:55 UTC — Temporary mitigation: revert tokenizer to version 2.13.7 in control plane for new worker launches and disable adaptive packer.
10:05 UTC — Rolling restarts performed on impacted worker pool onto previous image, throttling rollout.
10:25 UTC — Error rate begins to decline; autoscaler stabilizes.
11:40 UTC — Traffic back to baseline; monitoring confirmed normal p95 and error rate.
12:00 UTC — Incident declared resolved; post-incident actions started.
root_cause: A tokenizer change introduced an optimization that merged adjacent surrogate pairs and applied an alternate counting path for strings containing non-normalized Unicode sequences. For a subset of inputs (legacy-encoded chat histories and certain third-party client encodings), the optimized path returned a token count lower than the canonical encoder. The adaptive batcher uses the tokenizer-estimated token length to decide pack sizes; underestimated sizes caused the batcher to pack more requests than safe, which led to per-device memory oversubscription and GPU OOMs.
contributing_factors:
1) The canary rollout configuration allowed fast progression to 50% without a targeted encoding coverage test.
2) Adaptive packer heuristics lacked an upper safety cap per-request size and relied entirely on the tokenizer estimate.
3) Worker restart backoff logic retried on OOM quickly without circuit-breaking, causing repeated OOM cycles.
4) Streaming layer treated worker-side connection resets as transient and retried aggressively at the client-facing edge increasing load.
5) Telemetry did not expose token_count_estimate vs actual_tokenization delta; difference surfaced only after correlation.
detection_and_alerting: Primary alerts triggered were: hostedapi-5xx-rate-elevated and hostedapi-p95-latency-spike. These surfaced when customer-facing symptoms began. There was no dedicated alert for large token_count_estimate_delta. Post-incident we added a short-term synthetic monitor that compares tokenizer estimate vs canonical tokenization on a sample, with alert thresholds at 10% delta.
immediate_mitigation:
- Reverted tokenizer library on new worker launches to 2.13.7 (control-plane guardrail).
- Disabled adaptive packer (fallback to fixed max-batch-size) across all regions to stop dangerous packing behavior.
- Increased OOM backoff and introduced a short circuit at the autoscaler to prevent immediate re-launches onto the same faulty image.
- Edge retry rate cap applied to streaming sessions to reduce amplification from aggressive retries.
long_term_remediations:
1) Tokenizer QA: add a pre-release encoding sweep that runs canonical tokenization on a corpus of mixed encodings and measures estimate delta; failing builds blocked.
2) Batcher hard caps: enforce conservative per-request max_tokens safety cap (and an absolute batch memory estimator) that does not solely trust tokenizer estimates.
3) Telemetry: emit token_estimate_vs_actual metric sampled at 0.5% of requests for production; dashboard and alerting on >8% delta.
4) Worker resilience: implement a circuit-breaker for repeated OOM failures per image version on a host to avoid restart loops.
5) Rollout policy: change canary pipeline to hold at 25% for 30 minutes with targeted encoding coverage checks before wider rollout.
6) Streaming retry policy: exponential backoff + jitter and global backpressure-aware client-facing retry caps.
rollback_and_postmortem_notes:
Rollback was effective at halting new errors within ~10 minutes. The hottest period (09:35–09:55) produced the majority of customer-visible failures. We confirmed that no committed customer data was lost, but some streaming sessions were truncated and require customer-facing comms for high-volume users. The tokenizer PR has been updated with stricter normalization and a fallback conservative counting path; further tests were added in the PR.
We determined the immediate sequence would have been prevented if a synthetic token_estimate_delta test existed in pre-release and if the adaptive packer had a hard safety cap.

notes_to_oncall: If you see a sudden rise in GPU OOMs correlated with p95 latency and streaming reset spikes: 1) Check token_estimate_vs_actual sampling dashboard; 2) Disable adaptive packer via runtime flag (runtime flag: packer.disable_adaptive=true); 3) Revert to previous tokenizer image via control-plane pin; 4) Increase worker OOM backoff (oom.restart.backoff=30s) and open JIRA ticket and tag eng-serving-runtime. If repro is possible, capture sample inputs and upload to secure sandbox with scrubbing. Escalate to eng-serving-runtime on pager if errors persist > 15 minutes after mitigations.
post_incident_reflections: This incident sits at the intersection of a correctness regression (tokenizer) and an aggressive optimization (adaptive packer). We leaned on optimistic heuristics in multiple places without adequate cross-checks. The fix requires both better QA for upstream libraries and defensive limits inside runtime systems. The team demonstrated strong oncall triage and coordinated mitigation; timeline to final remediation must be prioritized to avoid recurrence.
